newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia mourns dead on Port Arthur anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Australia mourns dead on Port Arthur anniversary.

text.p: Australians on Monday held a national day of mourning on the anniversary of the country's worst modern-day massacre, when 35 people were shot dead by a lone gunman at the Port Arthur convict site.

Survivors and relatives of victims gathered for an emotional memorial service in the gutted remains of a 19th century sandstone church up a small hill from where gunman Martin Bryant began his deadly rampage on April 28, 1996.
"A year ago today the entire nation was shaken to its roots by the terrible tragedy at Port Arthur," Prime Minister John Howard said in a nationally televised address from Canberra.
"I hope that the lessons of Port Arthur will not be forgotten on the Australian community -- that there is a capacity for evil in our community..."
Only hours before the Port Arthur memorial service, Australian radio reported that Bryant, now serving a life jail sentence, had attempted suicide with an overdose of pills.

Bryant, 29, was found in his prison cell about two weeks ago suffering the effects of an overdose of medication and with a makeshift noose, made from torn sheets, lying among his bedding, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported.
The pills were supplied to him by another inmate at Risdon prison in Hobart, capital of the island state of Tasmania where the massacre took place, the unsourced radio report said.
Bryant is reported to have attempted suicide twice before, although prison authorities have declined to call them real attempts to end his own life.
But Australians on Monday expressed no sympathy for Bryant nor believed his anguish reflected contrition.
"I wouldn't like to assume that this apparent suicide attempt might indicate some act of contrition," said Ian Sale, the psychologist who exmained Bryant before his trial last year.
"I very much doubt that, I am afraid. You don't see redemption being an issue with that particular individual."

The nightmare of Port Arthur began on a crisp sunny autumn Sunday when Bryant left his meal in the Broad Arrow Cafe, took a semi-automatic rifle from his sports bag and calmly walked from table to table shooting at point blank range.

Those that begged for their life were targeted by a laughing Bryant. Within 15 seconds, 12 people were dead; within two minutes, 20. The carnage continued outside the cafe, as Bryant hunted down victims at random. Six-year-old Alannah Mikac had run behind a tree when Bryant put the gun to her neck.
"To my darling Lani, I can still hear your voice and smell your hair," Alannah's father Walter wrote on a wreath pinned on Monday to a twisted old gum tree near where she died.
By the time Bryant fled a burning cottage after an overnight siege with police, 35 people were dead, making his killing spree Australia's worst modern-day massacre.
Outrage at the massacre led to tougher gun laws in Australia which now ban semi-automatic weapons like that used by Bryant.

But the scars from that bloody Sunday remain raw for the small Tasmanian community. Local mayor Neil Noye told the 300 gathered at the convict church that today was "the anniversary of a day we would like to forget".
"What happened is beyond our understanding...even if we were to know, knowing would not make any difference," Noye said.

Speakers at the service said the anniversary represented the chance to finally reclaim the Port Arthur site, which was littered with flowers for those killed and a lonely wooden cross bearing the names of the dead.
Church leaders called for people not to dwell on the sorrow and hatred of the past, but to look to the future.

Like the tree that skeds its leaves in autumn, life would continue anew, said local Anglican priest Henry Levy, as Port Arthur was carpeted with maple leaves. Suvivors and relatives of victims have adopted the autumn maple leaf as their symbol.
"We have stood the force of the gale, the bushfire has raged around us, the drought has tested us, the frost has stunted us, and now we bear the scars," he said.
"The tree will again come into bud. This autumn leaf that we have is a sign of the past, and it is a promise of the future."
